AI for Mobility · Module 2 · Multimodal models

Camera, CAN and cross-attention: training a model that writes a crash warning

A 348,290-parameter multimodal language model reads 2 seconds of forward-camera video and 2 seconds of CAN bus data, then writes one line such as “lead vehicle braking . driver not braking . collision in 2 s”. It is small enough to read line by line and is trained with the same recipe as Flamingo. The data is synthetic: IDM car-following physics, rendered to a camera and a CAN log.

Two sensors, one sentence

A modern car already records two streams: a forward camera, and the CAN bus that carries speed, pedal positions, wheel speeds and the ACC radar's range to the car ahead. A human safety analyst watching both could write, in a few words, what is happening and what happens next. This page trains a model to do the same thing.

Pick a clip (test set, never seen in training)

Top: 8 frames, 4 per second, 48×48 px, grayscale. Bottom: the 7 CAN channels at 20 Hz, scaled to fit, on the same time axis. The last column is “now”.

Five scenarios, chosen so the evidence sits in different sensors

ScenarioWhat happensWhere the evidence isTest clipsEnd in a collision
Why synthetic? No public dataset has real crashes with synchronized video and CAN. SHRP2 does, under a data-use agreement. Here every clip comes from a simulator you already know: IDM for normal following, and for emergencies a driver reaction time plus a friction-limited deceleration a ≤ μg. The labels are exact, the physics is inspectable, and the simulator is ~400 lines in crash_scenarios.py. The price: the camera is a cartoon, and the model learns this simulator, not real roads (tab 7).

The report language

The sentence has three slots, scene . driver . outcome, over a vocabulary of 24 words. The training set has 41 distinct sentences across 10,000 clips. The outcome slot looks forward: whether the bumper-to-bumper gap reaches zero in the next 4 s, and if it does, in how many seconds (rounded up). Otherwise it reports “near miss” (gap under 2 m) or “no conflict”.

Cross-attention: the words ask, the sensors answer

Last week, self-attention let every word look at the words before it. A multimodal model needs one more move: the words must look at the sensor tokens. That is cross-attention. It uses the same dot product, the same scale and the same softmax. The difference is where the keys and values come from.

The key equation

CrossAttn(X, S) = softmax( (XWq) (SWk)T / √d ) · (SWv)

Symbols

  • X: the words written so far, one 64-number vector each. These give the queries.
  • S: the 136 sensor tokens (128 video patches and 8 CAN windows). These give the keys and values.
  • Wq, Wk, Wv: three learned 64×64 matrices, split into 4 heads of d = 16.
  • √d: the same scale as in the GPT, which keeps the softmax from collapsing onto one token.

In words: each word asks a question, every video patch and CAN window offers an answer, and the word takes a weighted average of the answers that fit its question.

Self vs. cross: the only differences

Self-attentionCross-attention
Queries fromwordswords
Keys, values fromthe same wordssensor tokens
Weight matrix12 × 12, square12 × 136, rectangular
Causal maskyes: no peeking aheadno: all 2 s of sensors are already in the past
Codeattn(x, x)attn(x, sensors)
In transportation terms, cross-attention is a query-dependent sensor fusion rule. A Kalman filter fuses radar and camera with weights set by noise covariances, fixed ahead of time. Here the weights are recomputed for every word. The word “slipping” can put its weight on the wheel-speed window where ABS kicked in, and the word “cutting” can put it on the frames where a car drifts across the lane line.

One detail from Flamingo: the gate

x ← x + tanh(α) · CrossAttn(norm(x), S) # α is one number per layer, starts at 0

With α = 0 the cross-attention adds exactly nothing, so the block is the unchanged language model. Training opens the gate only as far as the sensors lower the loss. This lets you bolt vision onto a pretrained LLM without first wrecking what it knows about language. Tab 3 shows the gates opening.

Going deeper (optional): why the gate starts at 0 rather than 1

At initialization the cross-attention output is noise: random Wq, Wk, Wv applied to tokens from an untrained encoder. With a gate of 1, that noise is added to every residual stream of a trained language model on the first step, and the gradients that follow partly undo its language skills. With tanh(0) = 0 the forward pass is exactly the pretrained model. The gradient on α is still non-zero (it is the dot product of the cross-attention output with the loss gradient), so the gate moves as soon as the sensor path carries information. Flamingo's ablations found the model trains worse without the tanh gate (Alayrac et al., 2022, section 3.3).

Three training stages: what is frozen when

Most production multimodal LLMs (Flamingo, LLaVA, Qwen-VL and the driving VLMs built on them) are trained in stages rather than all at once. The reason is cost: the language model is by far the most expensive part, so it is trained once on text and reused. This model follows the same recipe.

Green = trained in this stage. Gray = frozen. Dashed = not used.

Loss per word (training batches; dots = validation)

The two gates opening

Plotted as |tanh(α)|, one line per decoder layer. Both gates settled at negative values. The sign means nothing, because the output matrix Wo can flip it. What matters is that they left 0 the moment stage 2 began.

What each stage can do, on 3,000 test clips

Stage 1 is fluent and useless. Without the sensors it writes “lead vehicle braking . driver not braking . no conflict” for 100.0% of the test clips. Every sentence is grammatical, because the language model learned the report grammar. None of them is about the clip in front of it. That is the prior: the most common report in the data. A large LLM given a crash question and no image behaves the same way, just more eloquently.
Stage 2 does most of the work while the language model is frozen. Exact-sentence accuracy goes from 8.9% to 86.3%. The trainable part here (encoders, cross-attention, gates) is 70.6% of the parameters only because this language model is tiny. In real systems the LLM holds the vast majority of the parameters, which is exactly why it is frozen. Stage 3 unfreezes everything at a lower learning rate and adds a little more (87.0%).

Sizes: video encoder 110,400 · CAN encoder 102,400 · language model 102,336 · cross-attention layers incl. gates 33,026 · total 348,290 parameters. Training took 10 min on 2 CPU cores.

Watch each word look

These are the model's real cross-attention weights while it writes its report. Click a word and the frames and CAN windows light up according to how much weight that word's query put on them. The word below each token shows how much of its attention went to CAN.

Model wrote:
Shading is relative within each sensor: gold patches got more than the median video weight, and the darker CAN columns got more weight than the lighter ones (percentages at the bottom are of the word's total). The split between the sensors is in the numbers below.
Things to try. Each token shows the attention of the query that chose it. In a low_friction clip, click “wheels”, the point where the model decides between “driver braking” and “wheels slipping”. Its weight goes to CAN, because nothing in the image shows a wet road. In a cut_in clip, click “cutting”: the weight moves to the video, onto the patches where the merging car is. Then click the collision time (“1”, “2”…) to see which evidence the prediction uses, as distinct from the description. Last, click a word that grammar already forces, such as “slipping” right after “wheels”, or “s”. Nothing is left to decide, so where it looks means little.
Read attention maps with care. An attention weight shows where a query read from. It does not show what the model would do without that token. A word can spread its weight across many tokens and still depend on one. Tab 5 tests dependence properly by deleting a sensor.

Which sensor does each word need?

Averaged over all 3,000 test clips and both layers: the share of each word's cross-attention that lands on the 8 CAN tokens. CAN makes up 5.9% of the tokens (dashed line), so a word that ignored modality would sit on that line.

Measured with the true report fed in (teacher forcing). Each bar is the query that predicts the word shown. Words with fewer than 30 occurrences are omitted.
The bars that matter are the words where a decision is made. The first word picks the scene: “normal”, “stopped” and “lead” read mostly CAN, where radar range and closing speed separate them quickly, while “vehicle” (the start of “vehicle cutting in”) reads video. “wheels” vs. “driver” is decided from CAN. Words that grammar forces, such as “slipping” after “wheels” or “s” after the number, have nothing left to decide, and their attention wanders.

Delete a sensor, retrain, see what breaks

Attention shares show where a word reads. To test what the task needs, train the same model through all three stages with one sensor removed (245,890 parameters video-only, 237,890 CAN-only) and score it on the same test clips.

A sensor failure is a different test. Take the both-sensor model and mask its CAN tokens at run time, as if the CAN gateway dropped out, with no retraining. Its reports stay well-formed (100.0% are valid sentences), but it now catches only 35.1% of collisions, and says so just as fluently. Mask the video instead and only 0.1% of its outputs are even well-formed sentences. A fused model does not degrade gracefully to its better sensor unless it was trained with missing sensors (modality dropout).

Seconds of warning: against the classical baseline

A car with ACC already has a crash-warning rule: time-to-collision from the radar, range ÷ closing speed, and an alarm when it drops below a threshold. The threshold here, τ = 3.5 s, was tuned on the validation clips to maximize F1. If the multimodal model cannot beat this, it has no business in the car.

By scenario: where each method wins

Before you trust this result

  1. Baseline. Radar TTC with a tuned threshold, the rule in production cars, scored on the same clips. The text-only language model (stage 1) is the second baseline.
  2. Split. Train, validation and test clips come from different simulator seeds, so no trajectory appears in two sets. They do share one simulator, one camera and one set of physics. This is an in-distribution test and says nothing about real roads.
  3. Ugly cases. The model is only as good as the simulator's imagination: no rain, no night, no occlusion, no motorcycles, a cartoon camera. Some misses are irreducible, because the future depends on a reaction time that has not happened yet at “now”. And a generated sentence can be fluent and wrong, which no TTC rule can be.

Fit card: multimodal LLM for vehicle data

Idea in one sentence
Encode each sensor into tokens, then let a language model read them through cross-attention while it writes, so every word pulls evidence from whichever sensor answers its question.
Why it works
Attention weights depend on the query, so fusion is decided per word rather than fixed in advance. The gated, staged recipe lets a pretrained language model be reused without being retrained.
Fits these tasks
Explaining events in fleet video + CAN logs, triaging near-misses for safety analysts, answering questions about a drive, writing incident narratives. generation extraction classification
Needs this data
Time-synchronized video and CAN; sentences or Q&A describing clips (here, rule-generated; in practice, analyst narratives or LLM-drafted and human-checked); thousands of clips for alignment even at this toy scale.
Breaks when
Sensors fall out of sync; the camera or the CAN DBC changes between vehicle models; events are rarer than the training data allowed for; the text sounds confident about what it did not see (hallucination); latency: a report generated word by word is slower than one threshold.
Keep the classical method when
The decision is a single alarm with a hard deadline. Radar TTC is transparent, certifiable and runs in microseconds. Put the language model behind the alarm, for explanation, triage and review, unless it clearly beats TTC on the cases TTC misses and fails safe on the rest.

Where this shows up in practice

DomainTaskDataClassical baseline
Road safetyTriage a fleet's harsh-braking events: real conflict vs. a false triggerDashcam + CAN event snippets (telematics fleets, NDS data such as SHRP2)Deceleration threshold + manual video review
ADAS / driving automationExplain a disengagement or an AEB activation in words an engineer can fileCamera, CAN, planner logs (e.g. comma/openpilot drives)Rule-based event tagging
Agency practiceDraft the narrative field of a crash report from the vehicle's event data recorder + videoEDR pre-crash 5 s record, bodycam or dashcamOfficer-written narrative

Check yourself

  1. An OEM offers you 2 million hours of fleet CAN data and 40,000 hours of matching video. Only the video has been described in text by analysts. Which stage of this recipe does each dataset feed, and which modality will the model learn to under-use?
  2. Your agency wants an in-vehicle warning that sounds 2 s before rear-end crashes. Using tab 6, argue for or against putting this model in the warning loop, and say what you would put there instead.
  3. The attention map for “braking” lights up the brake-light pixels, but deleting the video barely changes the word. What does that tell you, and which of the two measurements do you trust for a safety case?
  4. You move this model from a sedan to a box truck with a higher-mounted camera. Which parts would you retrain, which would you freeze, and why does the staged recipe make that choice cheap?
Where the code and the numbers come from

crash_scenarios.py simulates the clips. multimodal_from_scratch.py is the model and the three training stages; its attention function is the same five lines as gpt_from_scratch.py. multimodal_numbers.py recomputes every number on this page. Nothing here is typed in by hand.

Reference: Alayrac, J.-B. et al. (2022). Flamingo: a visual language model for few-shot learning. NeurIPS. For the concatenation alternative (image tokens prepended to the text, no cross-attention): Liu, H. et al. (2023). Visual Instruction Tuning (LLaVA). NeurIPS.
